excerpt: Ordinary negligence is carelessness; gross negligence is conscious disregard. How that difference changes a car accident claim in Georgia and South Carolina.
keyTakeaways: Ordinary negligence is the failure to exercise reasonable care, while gross negligence involves conscious disregard for others' safety. Georgia recognizes three degrees of negligence under O.C.G.A. §§ 51-1-2 through 51-1-4 (§ 51-1-4 defines gross negligence). In Georgia, negligence, even gross negligence, does not support punitive damages; O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1(b) requires clear and convincing evidence of wilful misconduct, malice, fraud, wantonness, oppression or conscious indifference. Georgia caps punitive damages at $250,000 under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1, with no cap where the defendant intended harm or was substantially impaired by alcohol or drugs, or in product liability cases. South Carolina requires wilful, wanton or reckless conduct (S.C. Code § 15-32-520(D)) and caps punitive damages at the greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000 (indexed each year; $739,245 in 2026) under S.C. Code § 15-32-530. Georgia's comparative fault threshold is 50% (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33); South Carolina's is 51% (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.).

faqs.question: What is the legal definition of negligence in a car accident?
faqs.answer: Negligence is the failure to exercise reasonable care under the circumstances. In a car accident case, it means a driver did not act as a reasonably prudent person would — such as by speeding, running a red light, or driving distracted — and that failure caused your injuries.

faqs.question: How is gross negligence different from ordinary negligence?
faqs.answer: Gross negligence involves a conscious and voluntary disregard for the safety of others, while ordinary negligence is a simple failure to use reasonable care. Gross negligence reflects reckless behavior — such as extreme speeding, DUI at high BAC, or street racing — rather than mere carelessness or inattention.

faqs.question: Can I get punitive damages for gross negligence in Georgia?
faqs.answer: Not for gross negligence by itself. Georgia allows punitive damages only on clear and convincing evidence of willful misconduct, malice, fraud, wantonness, oppression or an entire want of care showing conscious indifference to consequences (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1(b)); the Supreme Court of Georgia has held that negligence, even gross negligence, is not enough (Colonial Pipeline Co. v. Brown, 258 Ga. 115 (1988)). Where punitive damages are awarded they are capped at $250,000 in most cases, with no cap where the defendant intended harm or acted while substantially impaired by alcohol or drugs (§ 51-12-5.1(f)), or in product liability cases (§ 51-12-5.1(e)).

faqs.question: What is the punitive damages cap in South Carolina?
faqs.answer: Under S.C. Code § 15-32-530, South Carolina caps punitive damages at the greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000, a floor indexed for inflation each year ($739,245 in 2026). The cap does not apply when the defendant intended to harm the plaintiff and did, pled guilty to or was convicted of a felony arising from the same conduct, or acted while impaired by alcohol or drugs to the degree that their judgment was substantially impaired (§ 15-32-530(C)).

faqs.question: Does Georgia or South Carolina have a more favorable comparative fault rule?
faqs.answer: South Carolina is slightly more favorable. Georgia bars recovery if you are 50% or more at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33), while South Carolina allows recovery as long as you are less than 51% at fault (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). A plaintiff who is exactly 50% at fault can recover in South Carolina but not in Georgia.

faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for negligence claims?
faqs.answer: In Georgia, the personal injury statute of limitations is 2 years from the date of injury under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33. In South Carolina, you have 3 years under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. These deadlines apply to both ordinary negligence and gross negligence claims.
